question: Why do different full-batch first-order optimizers appear to violate maximum-Hessian edge-of-stability thresholds by different amounts, and can stability be measured along the update direction the optimizer actually takes?

key_findings.claim: Maximum-curvature edge-of-stability scores have large, systematic optimizer-dependent offsets rather than hovering universally at one.
key_findings.evidence: Across 14 full-batch optimizer configurations on a 5-layer width-200 tanh MLP trained on all 50,000 CIFAR-10 examples, the interval-median relative edge chi ranged from 0.789 to 21.070. AdaGrad rose from 1.424 to 21.070 across its learning-rate grid; vanilla GD rose from 0.904 to 1.624, with four of five settings above one.

key_findings.claim: The paper generalizes the frozen-quadratic stability limit from standard momentum formulas to arbitrary causal gradient filters by using root-locus analysis.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 2.1 defines a filter-dependent escape gain from the first unit-circle crossing and proves the modal condition eta times lambda times Gamma at most two. It recovers Heavy Ball and Nesterov formulas when escape occurs at the Nyquist frequency, and also handles filters whose first crossing is elsewhere.

key_findings.claim: A realized edge measured along the optimizer's actual update removes most optimizer-family offsets and has an exact decomposition into worst-case, spatial, and temporal factors.
key_findings.evidence: The realized score is zeta = 1 + delta-L divided by eta times gradient-update alignment, equivalently curvature load divided by alignment. The identity zeta = chi times spatial participation divided by temporal calibration holds at every nondegenerate step. Reported family examples include GD chi 1.124 versus zeta 0.983, AdaGrad chi 21.070 versus zeta 1.002, and QHM zeta 1.000.

key_findings.claim: Worst-case edge and realized edge coincide only when spatial participation matches temporal calibration; occupying the top Hessian mode is sufficient in a special mode-locked quadratic regime but not generally necessary.
key_findings.evidence: Corollary 5.1 proves zeta equals chi if and only if spatial participation equals temporal calibration. For vanilla GD temporal calibration is identically one, so chi above one directly reflects updating in a direction with submaximal curvature. Theorem 5.3 shows eta, maximum sharpness, and filter gain cannot determine zeta without the missing ratio.

key_findings.claim: The realized score is far cheaper to measure than Hessian sharpness in the tested implementation.
key_findings.evidence: For one full-batch Adam step on a 777,000-parameter model with 50,000 examples and one RTX 5090, zeta required zero Hessian-vector products, 5.20±0.01 ms, and 305.4 MiB peak memory; the eight-step Lanczos chi estimate required eight Hessian-vector products, 110.15±2.56 ms, and 767.3 MiB. The authors report a 95.3% time reduction.

method.core_idea: Replace a worst-Hessian-mode stability certificate with a pathwise stability ratio computed on the optimizer's actual update ray, then factor the difference between the two scores into spatial and temporal diagnostics.
method.mechanism: The optimizer is written as a preconditioner applied to a causal filter of gradient history. Root-locus analysis supplies the exact frozen-quadratic escape gain Gamma for the temporal filter. Along the actual update direction, a secant Taylor expansion defines alignment A = gradient dot update and curvature load B. Their ratio zeta = B/A is the realized edge. Dividing directional curvature by maximum preconditioned sharpness gives spatial participation; comparing actual alignment with the filter's escape-mode alignment gives temporal calibration. The exact identity zeta = chi times spatial participation divided by temporal calibration diagnoses why worst-mode predictions miss.
assumptions: The exact realized-score interpretation uses deterministic full-batch loss and updates; stochastic minibatches change both the instantaneous landscape and the ratio.
The gradient filter is causal and its direct-current gain is normalized when comparing filter gains.
The alignment gradient dot update is nonzero when forming zeta and the decomposition.
The frozen-quadratic root-locus certificate describes local modal stability, while interpreting it as a nonlinear training attractor requires an additional occupation hypothesis.
The weighted secant Hessian along the finite update ray captures higher-order path effects relevant to that step.

techniques.role: Maps a causal gradient filter to the gain and frequency of its first unit-circle crossing, extending momentum stability thresholds beyond one-pole filters.
Measures integrated curvature along the actual finite update ray instead of assuming the optimizer travels in the maximum-Hessian eigenvector.
Uses gradient dot update as the loss-drop rate the optimizer attempts to realize, capturing temporal phase and preconditioning effects.
Decomposes realized stability into worst-case sharpness, participation in sharp directions, and calibration of the filtered update to its escape mode.
Computes zeta exactly for a full-batch step from current loss, next loss, gradient, update, and learning rate without Hessian-vector products.
Summarizes each trajectory by median chi between first entry above 0.75 and final exit below 0.75, avoiding long off-edge portions.

evaluations.setting: Deterministic full-batch CIFAR-10 training with a 5-hidden-layer, width-200 tanh MLP and 14 optimizer types; each family uses five geometrically spaced learning rates.
evaluations.metric: Median maximum-curvature relative edge chi over the edge-conditioned trajectory window.
evaluations.baseline: Classical and adaptive edge-of-stability theory predicts chi near or below 1.0.

evaluations.setting: Optimizer-family decompositions on the same full-batch CIFAR-10 trajectories.
evaluations.metric: Worst-case chi versus realized zeta, plus spatial participation and temporal calibration.
evaluations.result: Representative centers include GD 1.124 versus 0.983, Adam 0.960 versus 0.964, AdamW 0.971 versus 0.919, Heavy Ball 0.949 versus 0.983, AdaGrad 21.070 versus 1.002, and QHM zeta 1.000.
evaluations.baseline: Coincidence zeta = chi, which would require spatial participation to equal temporal calibration.

evaluations.setting: One full-batch Adam step, 777,000 parameters, 50,000-example batch, eight-step Lanczos comparison, RTX 5090.
evaluations.metric: Wall-clock time, Hessian-vector products, and peak device memory.
evaluations.result: Realized zeta: 5.20±0.01 ms, 0 HVPs, 305.4 MiB; chi: 110.15±2.56 ms, 8 HVPs, 767.3 MiB.
evaluations.baseline: Lanczos estimate of maximum preconditioned Hessian sharpness.

evaluations.setting: Exact frozen quadratic systems with general causal optimizer filters.
evaluations.metric: First root-locus crossing of the unit circle.
evaluations.result: The derived threshold eta-lambda-Gamma at most two is exact per eigenmode and recovers Heavy Ball and Nesterov Nyquist formulas as special cases.
evaluations.baseline: Earlier separable formulas restricted to particular momentum and preconditioner choices.

limitations: Author-stated: the theory and exact measurement focus on full-batch optimization; minibatch stochasticity makes alignment, curvature load, and their ratio random and requires an edge-of-stochastic-stability treatment.

Reviewer-identified: experiments use one small tanh MLP and CIFAR-10, so optimizer-family regularities are not yet established for transformers, normalization-heavy networks, or large-scale pretraining.
Reviewer-identified: the edge-conditioned median begins at a chosen chi threshold of 0.75 and can remain open at the training horizon; family summaries may depend on this window rule.
Reviewer-identified: zeta can be computed cheaply only after observing the loss at the updated parameters, so it is mainly diagnostic unless an optimizer accepts an extra or delayed loss evaluation.
Reviewer-identified: the spatial and temporal terms are exact algebraic channels, but the paper warns that changes in those channels should not automatically be interpreted as causal drivers.
failure_modes: When gradient-update alignment is zero or changes sign, zeta becomes undefined or loses the intended positive learning-power interpretation.
Noisy minibatch loss differences can make the ratio unstable, especially when the expected loss decrease is small.
A stale or mismatched loss evaluation breaks the exact finite-step identity used by the cheap estimator.
For rapidly changing adaptive preconditioners, a frozen-quadratic root-locus gauge can describe the filter but not the whole nonstationary optimizer state.
Near-singular temporal calibration can amplify the decomposition and make chi a poor proxy even when maximum sharpness is accurately estimated.
reusable_insights: Distinguish an available worst-case stability certificate from the direction the optimizer actually occupies.
Log-factorize multiplicative training diagnostics so spectral, spatial, and temporal deviations can be inspected on one additive stack plot.
Use loss decrease divided by gradient-update alignment as a cheap audit of how much intended first-order progress curvature dissipates.
Represent optimizer momentum as a causal filter and analyze its root locus; the first unstable frequency need not be period two.
For vanilla GD, a worst-mode stability score above one need not imply actual instability because the gradient can consistently point into lower-curvature directions.
open_questions: Can a low-variance estimator of realized zeta be derived for minibatch SGD and adaptive optimizers?
Do transformer pretraining trajectories exhibit the same optimizer-family offsets and spatial-temporal compensation?
Can zeta or its factors safely control learning rate online rather than only diagnose completed updates?
What mechanism makes optimizer trajectories select particular directional-curvature budgets near zeta equals one?
How should the framework handle negative alignment, saddle escape, or deliberately non-descent updates?

competitive_landscape.title: Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability
competitive_landscape.difference: Cohen et al. define the empirical full-batch GD edge through the maximum Hessian eigenvalue near two divided by step size; this paper argues that maximum curvature is only an available worst-case boundary and replaces it with curvature along the actual optimizer update.

competitive_landscape.title: Adaptive Gradient Methods at the Edge of Stability
competitive_landscape.difference: Cohen et al. extend the edge to adaptive preconditioners and momentum-specific stability thresholds; this paper generalizes temporal filters by root locus and shows that preconditioned maximum sharpness still has optimizer-dependent offsets unless spatial participation and temporal calibration are included.

competitive_landscape.title: Directional Smoothness and Gradient Methods: Convergence and Adaptivity
competitive_landscape.difference: Mishkin et al. develop path-dependent convergence bounds using directional rather than global smoothness; this paper incorporates directional secant curvature into an empirical edge-of-stability ratio and adds optimizer-state alignment plus an exact spatial-temporal factorization.

competitive_landscape.title: Edge of Stochastic Stability: Revisiting the Edge of Stability for SGD
competitive_landscape.difference: Andreyev and Beneventano replace full-batch maximum sharpness with expected minibatch directional curvature for SGD; this paper stays in deterministic full-batch optimization, covers many stateful optimizer filters, and explicitly leaves stochastic extension open.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper presents the realized edge zeta as a finite-step, optimizer-direction stability ratio, together with the exact decomposition zeta = chi times spatial participation divided by temporal calibration and a root-locus extension to general causal gradient filters.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Earlier primary work defines full-batch EoS with maximum Hessian curvature, extends it to adaptive preconditioned Hessians, studies directional smoothness for pathwise convergence, or treats stochastic batch sharpness. This paper unifies actual update direction and optimizer temporal state in one algebraic diagnostic and demonstrates large family-dependent corrections.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The formulation is technically distinct and diagnostically useful, but the broad empirical claim remains preliminary because all optimizer sweeps use one deterministic CIFAR-10 MLP. The theoretical generalization is strongest for fixed quadratics; its value for large nonstationary systems is currently empirical.

reviewer_notes: Author claim: realized zeta removes optimizer-dependent edge offsets and reveals how optimizers allocate spatial and temporal budgets. Reviewer inference: the algebraic decomposition is exact under its nondegeneracy assumptions, but interpreting its channels causally or extrapolating the observed family behavior beyond this architecture needs more evidence. Quantitative claims were checked against pages 5, 7-9, 27-28. Competitive-landscape metadata was checked against primary arXiv abstract pages.
